text.text: LucasArts and Factor 5 shed some light on Indy's transition to N64 in this site interview.

texts.text: Nintendo 64 has long been without an appropriate title to fill the genre gap opened with the omission of Lara Croft on the console. But that all looks to change this holiday when
and Factor 5 release

text.text: Indiana Jones and the Infernal Machine

texts.text: for purchase and rental at Blockbuster Video. The title, based on the PC version of the same name, features hours of puzzle-solving, exploration goodness, and a deep storyline to boot. We recently chatted with LucasArts and Factor 5 on just how difficult it was to bring the PC game home to N64, and what improvements have been made.

text.text: LucasArts officials first explained why the company decided to release Indiana Jones N64 as a Blockbuster Video exclusive:

texts.text: : LucasArts viewed the Blockbuster partnership as a very unique opportunity for this title. When we shared pre-release versions of Indy N64 with the people at Blockbuster, they were very excited about the potential of this title. Blockbuster has become a significant force in this industry -- particularly on the game rental side, which plays a large role in influencing video game customers. We looked at this as a tremendous way to provide special attention for this release.

text.text: With that explanation, read our full interview with co-developer Factor 5 on the title, below:
IGN64: How did the Indiana Jones port from the PC come to pass?

texts.text: : We looked at Indy progressing on the PC while working on Rogue Squadron. In fact, we had discussed the potential for a really nice N64 indoor engine back when Jedi Knight was nearing completion. Indy was such a natural for the N64 since there was no similar game in its genre on that platform and it posed an interesting technical challenge. When Rogue was finished, we created a prototype which convinced everybody involved that it would be possible. This of course was before the final development phase on the PC version, and the levels had grown considerably larger and more complex when we switched over to the final data at the end of 1999.

text.text: IGN64: So, how long did the Nintendo 64 version of the game in development from start to finish?

texts.text: : It was started in early March 1999 and finished in October 2000, so roughly 19 months.

text.text: IGN64: In between yourself and LucasArts how big was the team?

texts.text: : The core team consisted of 8 people, but we lured a lot of unsuspecting people into Indy 64 for certain periods of time. Almost every programmer here did something for it, artists from both Factor 5 and LucasArts did things here and there and on the LucasArts side the original level designers spent quite a bit of time just for the N64 version. LucasArts also had a great programmer dedicated to this version.

text.text: IGN64: What strengths and weaknesses did the N64 have when porting this game over from the PC?

texts.text: : The big strength was the N64 cartridge. We use the cartridge almost like normal RAM and are streaming all level data, textures, animations, music, sound and even program code while the game is running. With the final size of the levels and the amount of textures, the RAM of the N64 never would have been even remotely enough to fit any individual level. So the cartridge technology really saved the day.

text.text: In terms of weaknesses we fought hard against the fill-rate limitations of the N64. We loved Hi-Res on Rogue because of its crisp look, but the framerate was questionable. So when starting the engines for both Indy and Naboo, the main goal was to get a high framerate in Hi-Res. This meant not using the Z-Buffer, because it alone uses quite a bit of the N64's fillrate.
IGN64: We've noticed that the game has some really crisp textures. How did the team manage to get so much out of the N64?

texts.text: : We are using every trick possible in terms of optimal use of the 4K texture cache for every single texture. The programmers figured out the weirdest texture formats to get every texture to maximum resolution. An elaborate tool analyzes each original source texture and tries to come up with the best texture format for it on the N64. The tool also allows manipulating and choosing these texture formats by hand, something which we had to do in a lot of cases.

text.text: The sheer amount of textures was possible due to the streaming from the cartridge. While the player is running through the level, the program figures out which parts of the level need to be streamed in and does that in the background. So the amount of textures and size of levels is only limited by the cartridge, not the RAM of the N64. To achieve this, we had to rewrite not only all of the microcode but also quite a bit of the N64s operating system.
IGN64: Similarly, the lighting effects are also really good. Was this a goal of the team or did the engine willingly lend itself to this?

texts.text: : Real-time light was one of the areas that we improved upon from the PC version -- and this is an area that we usually emphasize in our games. So for Indy 64 it was immediately decided to do as much real-time light as possible, regardless of how much is there on the PC. This being the case, light is something the normal N64 microcode is not very good at. For Rogue we already had done some changes, but when we started Indy, we just started from scratch, threw away Nintendo and SGI's microcode and wrote everything from the ground up. Our new microcode allows almost unlimited real-time lights and a much higher polygon count than the original.

text.text: IGN64: Have you had to sacrifice anything of the PC version with the "port" to N64?

texts.text: : Nothing. Everything is there and so much has been added. Aside from the obviously rewritten control and camera to a completely new particle system with much better results up to new special weather, water, and real-time light effects, Indy 64 is quite a bit ahead of it's PC cousin in many ways. Even some of the animation was redone and new animation added for the analog control and the Z-targeting.

text.text: IGN64: How does Indy 64 differ from the PC version in terms of sound? What have you done in that respect?

texts.text: : The PC version had sampled MIDI-tunes for the music, something which helped us of course when we started the conversion. Added to those 128 pieces of music we composed a few new pieces just for the N64. On the sound effects side, Indy is a monster. More than 800 sound effects are featured in full environmental audio and Dolby Surround. To get the best quality for both music and FX, we went back to the original source files and redid the whole sound - in the end giving the N64 version a considerable improvement in sound quality compared to the PC.

text.text: IGN64: Exactly how are the controls changed from the PC version, and how did you decide to go with the N64 version's current control scheme?

texts.text: : To completely redo control and camera was one of the main points in early discussions with LucasArts. They saw the need for that as well, the N64 controller being vastly different to a keyboard on a PC. We started out by looking at Mario 64 and Zelda for inspiration. In addition, we had just created a prototype for our action game Thornado and for that already gathered some insight into the problems of a third person character game. In the end, though, it all came down to weeks and weeks of trying out camera and control behavior until everybody was satisfied. It certainly was tricky, since the levels were not originally built for a free-roaming camera, so we had to be especially careful about the movement of the camera through very narrow passages.

text.text: IGN64: Is there anything about the game that you wish you could have added in or had more time to smooth out?

texts.text: : There are of course some things you always have to let go when a product finally has to ship, but overall we are pretty happy with Indy. It certainly accomplishes most of the goals we set out to do when the project was started. It's a long, deep, and fun game and it pushes the N64 more than almost any other title, so one can't ask for much more.

text.text: IGN64: From a technical standpoint, what have you pulled off with Indy that most other N64 games simply aren't doing?

texts.text: : The high resolution and still having a really high framerate, the amount and resolution of the textures, the quality of the orchestral music and the environmental audio for sound effects, the real-time light and the particle system are the main technical qualities. You also get unlimited view-depth without any annoying fog.

text.text: IGN64: How many levels are featured in the game, and are there any special secrets to work toward?

texts.text: : There are 16 huge levels in the main story right away and for replay value the player can revisit all levels and hunt for treasures. If you collect enough treasures there is a really great bonus for them. In addition there are a few hidden option bits and pieces which are nice.

text.text: IGN64: Finally, how big is the cartridge?

texts.text: : 256 Megabits or 32 Megabytes with an Eeprom for Saving Games in the cart.

webpage.description:
My primary goal (or experiment) in this video was to
remove the limitations of the NES (and Famicom)
sound chips.

LINKS:
Akumajou Densetsu - Demon Seed
https://url.kylxbn.com/BDKKdp

I started with the triangle channel and was able to make
it output pure triangle waves. Then, I also modified the noise
channel so that it can output floating point samples.
However, the difference is extremely subtle, so I did not
demo it in this video. However, this is my subjective
opinion, but it now sounds closer to the noise output
of the Commodore 64's 6581 sound chip IN SOME INSTANCES.
I also tried to interpolate the DPCM channel linearly so that it
won't make huge steps up and down, but it proved to be
harder than I thought. Finally, I made some touches to the
mixing code so that all channels output floating point
data, all the mixing is performed using floating point
operations, and all the channels are mixed linearly. This
means that the triangle, noise, and DPCM channels
won't affect the volume of each other, which is often the
reason when the triangle, noise, or DPCM channels are
more quiet than the two square wave channels.

My second target was the VRC6. I spent three days trying
to interpolate the sawtooth channel linearly, encountering
a problem where a higher pitch results in a louder volume,
but it seems that I only had a problem with my interpolation
formula and I was able to fix it at day 3. Same with the
2A03, I made it so that all channels output floating point
values, and so that the mixer performs floating point
operations on them.

I also tried to improve the Namco N163 sound chip. Normally,
a sound chip would mix the output of each channel
via addition, and the result would be output 
44 to 48 thousand times per second. However, this
sound chip does not have a mixer at all. Instead,
the value of each channel is output in sequence like a
round robin. The more channels the N163 is working on,
the longer it takes for each channel to get its turn to output
its data, and this introduces aliasing noise to the output.
Fixing this should make it sound better theoretically, but
I have not implemented it yet so we will have to see in the 
future.

Finally, I had my eyes on the VRC7. The VRC7 is an OPLL
variant, and the OPLL does some operations using fixed point
values that would probably fare better using floating point
operations (like computing sine wave samples). However, this
proved to be daunting to implement, and it turns out that
just improving the digital-to-analog converter so that all
mixing operations are done using floating point operations
was enough to make the chip sound extraordinarily good.

Doing all these fixes were tiring and it took me a lot of time.
But the result was very much worth it. Listening to some
famous NES soundtracks like Megaman, Castlevania 3,
Journey to Silius, Ninja Gaiden, and Gradius II, I can
definitely say that there IS an improvement.

Feel free to request any song in the comments section
that you might want to hear using an improved
NES sound chip!

text.text: Saving video gaming’s source code treasures before it’s too late
Over 90 percent of pre-2000 gaming source code may already be gone.

texts.text: When most people think of
, they probably imagine a museum full of boxed consoles and cartridges, or maybe

text.text: a massive, digital database of emulatable ROM files

texts.text: ripped from the original physical media. The Video Game History Foundation's
is looking past those kinds of basic archival projects, though, and toward collecting and preserving the source code behind many classic games.

text.text: "For a video game historian, an archaeological dig through source material is the next best thing to time travel,' VGHF's Frank Cifaldi said. "A really good source repo is the closest you're ever going to get to being a fly on the wall during a game's development."

texts.text: Digging through a game's source code repository can help archivists discover previously unknown content and information. Back in 2017, for instance, a VGHF analysis

text.text: found unused Disney character art and animation

texts.text: in the source code for 1993's Genesis
game ("Some of that was in a folder called trash," Cifaldi told Ars). More recently, the VGHF team discovered the source code for
—a game prototype for the unreleased Sega Genesis virtual reality headset—and

text.text: remade it to work on modern VR hardware

But it's not just about finding and restoring "lost" content. Looking at source code can let a knowledgeable historian "understand the creative process a lot better than you would otherwise because it is the purest form of the game," Cifaldi said. "It is the raw building block that made it up."

texts.text: By way of example, Cifaldi talked about his time looking at the source code for
and learning the language and tools behind

. "Now when I play a SCUMM game, I understand it a little more. I speak the language a little better," he said. "In knowing SCUMM, I just have this intuitive understanding of why creative decisions were or weren't made in its game, and I don't think I could possibly have that level of understanding without access to SCUMM language."
Unfortunately, games like

(where creator Ron Gilbert maintained and generously donated the source code) are the exceptions. For games made before 2000, Cifaldi estimates that the source code is completely gone for over 90 percent of "the games we care about."

text.text: "I'm sure a lot of source was saved at one time, then an office move happened, someone said, 'What's this old DAT we have in a closet? It's probably backed up somewhere, just toss it,'" Cifaldi said. "I think the situation is pretty bad. It's only going to get worse as the people who actually archived this stuff age out and leave the industry, if not this mortal coil."

texts.text: Footage of a cut Sword Swallower enemy that was restored to 1993's
Genesis game from the source code.

When early game source code survives, Cifaldi said it's often by pure happenstance, "individuals who maybe brought their work home and happen to have that material." The source code for a previously unknown
prototype on the NES, for instance,

by digging through "a pile of floppy disks in the basement of its deceased developer," as Cifaldi recalls. He imagines there are "hundreds more [game source code repositories] like that, just floppies rotting in someone's basement waiting for someone to recover."

text.text: That's why VGHF is putting out the call to developers who may have these important historical artifacts among their possessions. While the project is in its early days, Cifaldi said the foundation currently has about 100 titles with source code repos "in various states," including some that are just printouts on endless reams of paper.

Even when the source code does still exist, preservationists often run into problems with protectionist companies trying to jealously guard their IP rights. "[Source code is] seen as a trade secret, and there's no statute of limitation on when people are comfortable with a trade secret," Cifaldi said.

texts.text: It's hard to talk about game history and trade secrets these days without addressing

text.text: the "Gigaleak" of Nintendo prototypes and unused designs

texts.text: that hit the Internet in July 2020. Cifaldi said that this kind of leaking of closely guarded company secrets is "not something that we're trying to encourage. We're not asking people to conduct commercial theft for the sake of preservation necessarily, but it's something we have to be cognizant of."

text.text: Cifaldi was particularly distressed that the leak included potentially embarrassing personal details, like naughty words used in source code snippets or emails between developers. "That's immature of the individual to do that, but it also reflects an immaturity in the public understanding of how games are made and that things can get a little messy."

That kind of stuff getting out "potentially could hinder efforts like ours" to preserve things legitimately, Cifaldi said. At the same time, "those leaks, the good side of it is that it is sparking imaginative conversation among fans and historians about the making of Nintendo's products. It is giving people a much clearer understanding of the game development process than they might have had in the past, which I'm always a fan of."

texts.text: Convincing companies to share those "secrets" for historical posterity—and to spend the time and effort looking for it in the first place—can be an uphill battle, Cifaldi said. But that's starting to change in some corners, in part because of

text.text: the industry-wide trend toward remakes and remasters

texts.text: for well-remembered games.
In the case of a game like

, for instance, "the only reason that product exists is because employees had things in their houses and people know who to ask," Cifaldi said. Without the source code, doing that kind of remastering work is a much bigger lift—when Cifaldi worked at Digital Eclipse, none of the games had available source code, meaning the team

text.text: had to create an entirely new engine and reverse-engineer the games

texts.text: from extant ROM files.
Companies are starting to cotton on to the value of this kind of preservation, though. Disney started to realize the value of source code preservation, for instance, when it used that raw material in
2019's collection of remastered
and
games

text.text: "In all cases, there is interest internally because a lot of the companies we've spoken to have recognized that it sparks fan interest if people are talking about these older products," Cifaldi said. "A lot of commercial film preservation, remastering movies for Blu-ray or whatever, a lot of that happens because the Library of Congress has the master film reel in its archives... The idea of video game source repositories is to me no different than that."

texts.text: Commercial re-releases aside, though, Cifaldi said the source preservation project is seeking to provide the raw materials necessary for continued scholarship on classic games. He likened it to the documents and letters that serve as the basis for civil war histories or the archived production materials that illuminate the creation of

text.text: "We want to see more books on bookshelves, more documentaries out there, more in-depth study than we're currently seeing," Cifaldi said. "Source repositories like this, this is where history books come from."

The S.S.T. Band was Sega's official in-house band from 1988 to 1993, specializing in rock versions of soundtracks of Sega's arcade games, for collection albums and playing in festivals. Consisting of six members, the band consisted of members that included keyboardist Hiroshi Kawaguchi, Katsuhiro Hayashi, and Kimitaka Matsumae, guitarists Koichi Namiki and Jouji Iijima, bassists Sachio Ogawa and Shingo Komori, drummer Takehiko Tanabe. Miyauchi and Komori would leave the band in 1990 and be replaced by keyboardist Takenobu Mitsuyoshi and bassist Masato Saito.

Usually, some of these albums that were released would consists of two especially recorded versions of the game soundtrack and the rest would consist of the game's original soundtrack. After the band members went their own ways, they would find themselves involved in other Sega projects. Mitsuyoshi would be responsible for the soundtrack to Virtua Fighter, Daytona USA and the two installments of Shenmue and Matsumae would be involved in Sega Rally and Virtua Fighter 3.

Speedrun vérifié, chronométré et accepté par Speed Demos Archive le 19 Décembre 2012. Effectué sur la version PC 15th Anniversary au clavier, le 14 Octobre 2012.

Enregistré avec Fraps.

Il m'aura fallu 3 mois et 11 jours pour en arriver à cette performance, soit 408 tentatives de passer à 5:07 sans mourir (possibilité basée uniquement sur de la chance). Parmi ces 408 essais, seulement 9 m'ont accordé la survie, la 7ème de ces opportunités fut un succès mais je décidai de recommencer le run en raison de quelques erreurs de maladresse. 168 essais plus tard, voilà enfin le résultat que j'attendais.

Voici donc le nouveau record mondial sur Another World 15th Anniversary, réalisé en 8 minutes 03 entre le moment où je prends le contrôle de Lester jusqu'à mon dernier input. Je ne remercierai jamais assez Archanfel pour son aide et son soutien tout au long de ces 3 mois. Ce dernier a récemment réalisé un speedrun segmenté de Bermuda Syndrome, un jeu PC très inspiré à la fois de Another World et de Prince Of Persia.

Voici le lien: https://www.youtube.com/watch?feature=player_embedded&v=Xee5EJ7_cgY

Merci aussi à Eric Chahi pour ce chef d'oeuvre intemporel et merci au forum SDA !

Continuando a minha investigação sobre música no TRS Color, eu consegui o formato da onda usado para gerar o som de órgão:
Em tese se quiser gerar o som de outro instrumento, basta trocar os samples
Eu acho bem difícil fazer ritmos mais "funky" em trackers.
Forma de onda com 256 amostras? Suntuoso! 😁
sim, bastante
parece simples de representar como uma soma ponderada de muito poucas senóides
E o lance que eu estava achando estranho e que entendi foi o seguinte:
Parece simples mesmo, ainda mais considerando que daria pra fazer algo mais complexo
se é PCM poderia ser qualquer bagunça doida que o autor quisesse

Basicamente para tocar as notas o código faz o seguinte:
1. Inicializa 4 ponteiros na tabela de sample
2. Para cada linha do "tracker", pega-se a duração e as notas de cada canal
3. Pega-se o sample de cada canal e os soma
4. Pega-se o resultado e toca-o no DAC
5. A informação da nota diz qual passo deve ser utilizado para pular o ponteiro da tabela de sample
6. O ponteiro é ajustado conforme o passo (nota)
7. Repete-se os passos de 3 a 6 até a duração terminar

O que eu estava achando estranho é que o passo é 16 bits, até aí tudo bem. Mas na hora de atualizar o ponteiro, ele fazia assim:
                ldd     MVoice1+1
                addd    MInc1
                std     MVoice1+1
D é um registrador 16 bits (na verdade é a junção dos registradores acumuladores A e B, pensem no H e L do Z80)
O ponteiro para a voz1 é o MVoice1
eu pensando "ué, não era para ser MVoice1 apenas? Por que esse +1?"

Lá na definição do MVoice1 (e dos outros, aliás), acabei descobrindo o lance: eles não são 16 bits, mas 24 bits! Na verdade 16.8 bits:
         MVoice1         rmb     3
Os incrementos são 16 bits justamente para pegar os 8 bits da parte "inteira" do ponteiro e os 8 bits da parte "fracionária" do ponteiro]
Aí na hora de ler o sample, ele usa apenas os 16 bits da parte "inteira". Por sinal a tabela de samples está no endereço $3E00 , justamente para que o byte mais significativo do endereço não mude
Fiz alguns experimentos agora: coloquei uma onda quadrada e depois uma onda triangular
